title: Jaap close
hook: the Tenth Guru's praise now sits beside Nanak's Japji in your morning

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam, and your line, all the names: the whole hymn, start to finish. Today, the last of our thirty days with Jaap Sahib.

Some mornings have a shape you'd recognize in the dark. Feet on the cold floor. Water on the face. The kettle, the same mug. In Sikh homes that keep Nitnem, the shape has words too, in a fixed order. First a quiet, thoughtful voice, the first Guru's. Then a faster one, written generations later, with a drumbeat in it. Thirty days ago you only knew the first.
screen: `A MORNING YOU'D KNOW IN THE DARK.` → `FIRST A QUIET VOICE.` → `THEN A FASTER ONE WITH A DRUMBEAT.`

segments.voice: Put the two side by side. Japji is Guru Nanak's, the first Guru, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib on page one. Jaap is Guru Gobind Singh's, the tenth Guru, and it opens the Dasam Granth. Two first pages, two Gurus many generations apart. Japji begins with Ik Onkar, One, and the Mool Mantar: true Name, creator, without fear, without hatred, timeless, unborn. Jaap begins with no mark, no caste, then salutes the One as akaal, abhai, ajooni. Same truths, different walk. Japji thinks its way forward, pauri by pauri, asking questions. Jaap marches, name after name, through many meters and languages. Sikhs believe the same light, the same jot, passed from Guru Nanak to each Guru in turn. Saying Japji and then Jaap each morning is a small way of hearing that: the first Guru's voice, then the tenth, and the light in both. Now look back at the road. The morning praise, Jaap Sahib. No mark, no caste. King of kings. Named by deeds. The snake's gait. Akaal, the Timeless. The Merciful. Formless, beyond compare. Ajooni, unborn. The armed One, the protector. Sun of suns. Song of songs. The lamp of beauty. The provider. Gobind. One form, many sights. Ender and sustainer. Karunaa, the house of compassion. Breaker of the cruel. The one-letter meter. Abhai. Every land. Beyond the fear of death. Keeping the pace. The last stanza. The amrit bowl. Courage. So many names. The whole Jaap. Tomorrow, the third morning bani: ten verses under the heading by your grace.
screen: `JAPJI OPENS ONE GRANTH, JAAP THE OTHER.` · `THE FIRST GURU, THEN THE TENTH.` · `ONE LIGHT, ONE JOT, IN BOTH.` · `THIRTY DAYS OF NAMES.` · then, large: `JAPJI, THEN JAAP.`

segments.voice: Picture tomorrow morning: where you'll be, what you'll do first, and the place where a few lines of Jaap could go. A recording while you dress, the four words ajai, alai, abhai, abai at the window, or the full fifteen minutes if your life allows. Choose one, gently, and rest.
Nitnem, the daily rule of prayer. After thirty days, the Tenth Guru's morning praise sits beside Guru Nanak's Japji: the first Guru's voice, then the tenth.
Your line: japji, then jaap. One light, heard in both voices each morning. Jaap, done.

screen: `DAY 361 COUNTS.` → `JAAP SAHIB, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: BY YOUR GRACE.`

howItsDone: In the Sikh morning Nitnem, Japji Sahib is recited first and Jaap Sahib second, followed by the Tav Prasad Savaiye; many Sikhs say all three before or around dawn.

what it means: it pairs the Tenth Guru's voice with the first Guru's, the same light heard twice every morning.
what a scholar hears: both banis open their scriptures, and Jaap's akaal, abhai and ajooni restate the Mool Mantar's akaal moorat, nirbhau and ajooni.

chat.says: You say two morning prayers now? Which comes first, and why that order?
options: Japji, Guru Nanak's, then Jaap, the Tenth Guru's: one light in both voices.
Jaap first, since the Tenth Guru's drumbeat wakes you up before Japji.
Either one; Nitnem has no set order, so pick whatever suits the morning.
